title: A Lonely Spiral in a Tapestry of Galaxies
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3198, imaged by the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope
credit: KPNO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA. · Acknowledgments: PI: M T. Patterson (New Mexico State University) Image processing: Travis Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage), Mahdi Zamani & Davide de Martin

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The spiral galaxy NGC 3198 appears in full in this image, from its bright central bulge out to the faint edges of its tightly wound arms. The galaxy sits in the constellation Ursa Major, about 47 million light-years away.

Almost everything in the background is a galaxy or galaxy cluster, a sea of distant galaxies in every shape, size and orientation. NGC 3198 itself has helped astronomers with the old problem of measuring distances accurately. Working out how far away anything is, from the Sun to remote galaxies, takes a combination of measurements and methods.

NGC 3198 allowed astronomers to calibrate distance measurements based on Cepheid variables, a type of pulsating star. Cepheids brighten and dim with a period linked to their true brightness, so comparing how bright one really is with how bright it appears reveals its distance. The Mosaic camera on the Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory recorded the galaxy.
scale: NGC 3198 lies about 47 million light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: Taken with the Mosaic camera on the NSF Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter Telescope through U, B, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
